text_blocks.text: You have studied linear equations in one variable in the previous classes. Recall that a linear equation in one variable is an equation involving only linear polynomials in one variable. Thus, equations of the form ax = b, ax + b = c, ax + b = cx + d (where a != 0, b, c, d are constants) are linear equations in one variable. For example, x + 2 = 0, 2x - sqrt(3) = 0, 5x + 3 = 3x - 5, y/3 - 3 = y/3 + 3 etc. are linear equations in one variable. You also know that such equations have a unique (i.e. one and only one) solution. Now, let us see some examples of solving linear equations in one variable (i.e. finding the value of the variable satisfying the equation).

text_blocks.text: Let us now consider the statement 'The sum of two numbers is 10'. If we denote the first number by x and the second number by y, then the statement can be expressed as 'x + y = 10'. This is a linear equation in two variables (x and y). Likewise 3x + y = -5, 2u - v = 4, -4x + 3y = 9, x/3 + y/4 = 1 etc. are all linear equations in two variables. Thus, a linear polynomial in two variables equated to zero gives a linear equation in two variables. It is also called a first degree equation in two variables.
The general form of a linear equation in two variables is ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are constants and a, b are both non-zeroes.

If either a = 0 or b = 0, the equation ax + by + c = 0 is no more a linear equation in two variables in its most general form. But in some special circumstances, either a or b is granted to be zero. For example, the equation 3x + 2 = 0 can be written in the general form as 3x + 0.y + 2 = 0.

You have already known that every linear equation in one variable has a unique solution. What can you say about the solution of a linear equation in two variables? If the two variables be x and y, then a pair of values, one for x and one for y which satisfy the equation is called a solution of the equation.

This solution is written as an ordered pair (3, 1). In such an ordered pair the first component invariably represents a value of x and the second, the corresponding value of y. Similarly, the ordered pair (2, 4) is also a solution of the equation 3x + y = 10. But (2, 5) is not a solution of this equation, because on putting x = 2 and y = 5, we get 3x + y = 6 + 5 = 11 != 10.

You have already seen two solutions of the equation 3x + y = 10 viz. (3, 1) and (2, 4). You can also verify that (0, 10) is also another solution of the equation. In fact, we can get many solutions of the equation by assigning different values to x (or y) in the equation and finding the corresponding value of the other.

worked_examples.problem: Write each of the following equations in the form ax + by + c = 0 (a > 0) and indicate the values of a, b and c in each case: (i) 3x - 4y = 5, (ii) x + 5 = 2y and (iii) 3x = y.
steps: (i) The equation 3x - 4y = 5 can be written as 3x - 4y - 5 = 0, which is of the form ax + by + c = 0. Here a = 3, b = -4 and c = -5.
(ii) The equation x + 5 = 2y can be written as x - 2y + 5 = 0, which is of the form ax + by + c = 0. Here a = 1, b = -2 and c = 5.
(iii) The equation 3x = y can be written as 3x - y + 0 = 0, which is of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a = 3, b = -1 and c = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Write each of the following as an equation in two variables: (i) 4x = 3, (ii) x = -2, (iii) 2y = 5
steps: (i) 4x = 3 can be written as 4x + 0.y - 3 = 0.
(ii) x = -2 can be written as x + 0.y - 2 = 0 (or x + 0.y + 2 = 0).
(iii) 2y = 5 can be written as 0.x + 2y - 5 = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Find any three different solutions for each of the following equations: (i) 2x + 3y = 6, (ii) 3x + 4y = 0, (iii) 2x + 5 = 0.
steps: (i) Taking x = 0, the equation 2x + 3y = 6 reduces to 3y = 6, which gives y = 2. Therefore, (0, 2) is a solution of the equation.

text_blocks.text: Similarly, taking y = 0, the given equation reduces to 2x = 6, which gives x = 3. So, (3, 0) is also a solution of the given equation. Again, taking x = 6, we get 12 + 3y = 6 i.e. y = -2. (6, -2) is also another solution of the equation. Hence, three solutions of the equation 2x + 3y = 6 can be given as (0, 2), (3, 0) and (6, -2).

(ii) Taking x = 0, the equation 3x + 4y = 0 reduces to 4y = 0 i.e. y = 0. So, (0, 0) is a solution of the equation 3x + 4y = 0. Again, taking x = 4, we get 12 + 4y = 0 i.e., y = -3. Therefore, (4, -3) is a solution of the given equation. Similarly, taking y = 3, we get 3x + 12 = 0 i.e., x = -4. So, (-4, 3) is also another solution of the equation. Hence, three solutions of the given equation are (0, 0), (4, -3) and (-4, 3).
(iii) Writing the equation 2x + 5 = 0 as 2x + 0.y + 5 = 0, we obtain x = -5/2 for any value of y. Hence any three solutions of the given equation are (-5/2, 0), (-5/2, 1) and (-5/2, 2).

text_blocks.text: From the previous article you know that a linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions and you have obtained some of these solutions algebraically so far. Now, let us look at their geometrical representation. Consider the following equation: 2x + 3y = 12 ... (i)

Some of the solutions of this equation are (0, 4), (6, 0), (3, 2), (-3, 6). The points represented by these ordered pairs are plotted in the cartesian plane. Joining any two of these points we obtain a straight line AB (Fig. 4.1). Also we see that the other two points lie on the line AB.

Now, let us take a point on this line, say P. On finding the co-ordinates of P, we find the ordered pair (9, -2). We see that (9, -2) is a solution of the equation for x = 9 and y = -2 satisfy the equation. Similarly, the co-ordinates of any other point on the straight line AB may be shown to satisfy the equation. But the co-ordinates of a point which is outside the line AB do not satisfy the equation.

Thus, we observe that (i) every point whose co-ordinates satisfy equation (i) lies on the line AB; (ii) the co-ordinates of every point on the line AB constitute a solution of equation (i); and (iii) the co-ordinates of any point which does not lie on the line AB do not constitute a solution of equation (i).

headings: 4.4 Graph of a Linear Equation in two Variables

text_blocks.text: So, the linear equation (i) is geometrically represented by the line AB. This line is called the graph of the linear equation. Thus, we conclude that the graph of a linear equation is a straight line whose points make up the aggregate of solutions, of the equation. To obtain the graph of a linear equation in two variables, it is enough to plot two points corresponding to two solutions of the equation and draw a line through them. However, it is better to plot at least three such points so that you can immediately check the correctness of the graph.

worked_examples.problem: If the work done by a constant force acting on a body is directly proportional to the distance travelled by the body...
steps: Here the variables involved are distance and work. Let x be the distance travelled by the body and the work done by the force be y units.
It is given that y is directly proportional to x (y \propto x).
If k be the constant force acting on the body (which is also the constant of proportionality), then y = kx, which is the linear equation representing the given statement.
If k = 2 units, the above equation becomes y = 2x.
To draw the graph of this equation, we take some of the ordered pairs satisfying the equation as given below: (0,0), (2,4), (4,8), (5,10), (-1,-2).
worked_examples.final_answer: y = 2x. From the graph, when distance x = 5 units, work done y = 10 units.
